introduction-the-decentralized-machine.core: Nobody owns the internet, but someone must coordinate the unique identifiers (IP addresses, AS numbers, DNS root and protocol parameters) or it would collide into chaos. That coordination is layered: IANA, under ICANN, keeps the global pools; five Regional Internet Registries allocate to networks; the IETF sets protocols; and thousands of independent operators connect by commercial agreements and BGP.

first_principles.problem: An engineer assumes a government 'runs the internet' and is confused about who to ask for IP space.

analogy.title: International postal coordination
analogy.story: A union assigns country codes; each country runs its own postal service and agrees how mail is exchanged.
analogy.breaks: Postal unions are treaty-based; internet governance is largely voluntary and multi-stakeholder.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Traces allocation to an RIR and organisation.

code.text:
whois 8.8.8.8 | grep -iE 'NetRange|OrgName|source'
# NetRange: 8.8.8.0 - 8.8.8.255
# OrgName: Google LLC
# (ARIN)

check.q: Who allocates IP addresses to an ISP in Europe?
check.a: RIPE NCC, the Regional Internet Registry for Europe, Middle East and parts of Central Asia.

iana-the-keeper-of-the-root.core: IANA, operated by PTI under ICANN since the 2016 stewardship transition, performs three functions. It keeps the global IP address and ASN pools, allocating large blocks to RIRs; it manages the DNS root zone (which TLDs exist and their name servers), with Verisign publishing it to the 13 root server identities; and it maintains protocol parameter registries (port numbers, HTTP status codes) for the IETF.

first_principles.problem: A team wonders who decides that port 443 means HTTPS and who adds a new TLD.
derivation: Root servers **publish** it (13 identities, many anycast instances).

analogy.title: The master copy of a dictionary
analogy.story: One authority keeps the official word list and definitions; publishers distribute copies worldwide.
analogy.breaks: Dictionaries evolve slowly; protocol registries update constantly.

code.text:
dig . NS +short | sort | head -3
# a.root-servers.net.
# b.root-servers.net.
# c.root-servers.net.

check.q: Are there really only 13 DNS root servers?
check.a: There are 13 root server identities (a–m), but each is served by many anycast instances, over 1,700 worldwide.

rirs-the-regional-distributors.core: Five RIRs (AFRINIC, APNIC, ARIN, LACNIC, RIPE NCC) allocate IP addresses and ASNs to members (ISPs, enterprises, clouds) under community-developed policies. IPv4 is exhausted at all RIRs, so new IPv4 comes from waitlists, small final allocations, or transfers on a market where addresses sell for tens of dollars each. IPv6 is plentiful. RIRs also run WHOIS/RDAP, IRR databases and RPKI trust anchors.

first_principles.problem: A start-up expanding to multi-homing learns it can't simply request a /22 of IPv4 from its RIR.
truths: RIRs anchor registry data and RPKI.
derivation: Obtain **IPv4 via transfer market** or lease.

analogy.title: Regional land registries after the land ran out
analogy.story: New plots aren't issued anymore; you buy from existing owners, with the registry recording the transfer.
analogy.breaks: Land is physical; IPv6 makes 'land' effectively unlimited.

example.title: RDAP lookup
example.outcome: how to get and manage number resources.

check.q: How do organisations get new IPv4 space today?
check.a: Mostly via the transfer market or leasing, since RIR free pools are exhausted (with small waitlist allocations).

bgp-the-protocol-that-holds-the-internet.core: Governance assigns identifiers, but BGP makes them reachable. Each AS announces the prefixes it holds, and neighbours pass them on according to business relationships. The global table (about 1 million IPv4 and 200,000 IPv6 prefixes) is the emergent result of tens of thousands of independent policy decisions, with no central controller, and that is both its resilience and its fragility.

first_principles.problem: An organisation gets IP space from its RIR but users still can't reach it.

analogy.title: Owning a house vs being on the map
analogy.story: Owning the land doesn't help if your street isn't on any map; announcements put you on it.
analogy.breaks: Maps update yearly; BGP updates in seconds.

check.q: Why might an upstream ignore your new prefix announcement?
check.a: Its filters only accept prefixes with matching IRR route objects (and valid ROAs), which you haven't registered yet.

bgp-peering-politics-the-business-of-con.core: Networks connect in two main ways. Transit means a customer pays a provider for reachability to the whole internet. Peering means two networks exchange traffic between their own customers, often settlement-free, at IXPs or via private interconnects. Tier-1 networks reach everyone without buying transit. Peering decisions are business negotiations about traffic ratios, footprint and who benefits.

first_principles.problem: A growing video platform's transit bill climbs to $200k/month and it wants to know how to cut it.
truths: Value depends on traffic balance and reach.

analogy.title: Toll roads vs neighbourly shortcuts
analogy.story: You pay tolls to use the motorway (transit), but agree with a neighbour to share a private lane between your properties (peering).
analogy.breaks: Neighbours share for goodwill; peering disputes are business leverage.

check.q: What routes does a peer typically exchange?
check.a: Only its own and its customers' routes, not routes learned from its other peers or providers.

when-peering-goes-bad-de-peering-events.core: De-peering is when a network ends a peering relationship, usually over a traffic-ratio or payment dispute. If neither side has transit covering the other, single-homed customers of each lose reachability to each other: an internet partition. Historical disputes (Level 3 vs Cogent, Cogent vs Sprint) cut off parts of the internet for days. Multi-homing with diverse transit is the defence.

first_principles.problem: Customers of one ISP suddenly can't reach a cloud provider's region because the two networks de-peered.
truths: Some networks rely solely on peering for certain routes.

analogy.title: Two bridges closing over a toll dispute
analogy.story: Towns connected only by that bridge are cut off until the owners settle.
analogy.breaks: Bridges can't be rerouted; networks can buy transit, if they choose to.

example.title: Detect a partition
flow: AS174 vantage points fail to reach origin
Shift announcements to a different upstream

check.q: Why can de-peering partition the internet?
check.a: If two networks reach each other only via that peering and neither buys transit covering the other, their customers lose mutual reachability.
